utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know about these three and the other one, but do you know anything about Pakrac Marino Selo the administration building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was all a single camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know anything about the Pakrac Ka Poljana camp in the Jedinstvo company? This was a company producing ballpoint pens and light switches.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this can be considered a single camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then the fishing cottage and the firefighting centre, the fire brigade centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all a single location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the other locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all a single camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many Serbs were detained in those camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the number is. They said it was over a hundred. Some said two or three hundred, but we never got any exact data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you speak of a hundred, two hundred, or three hundred, are you speaking of all the camps you confirmed existed in Pakrac and in the Pakrac region, or in one of these camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said refers to Pakrac Ka Poljana. As for the basement of the Pakrac department store, I don't know the number detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know how many people were there, but you know there was a camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because people are still afraid to speak about it, the people who were there, at least those that I'm in contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you are now in contact. We heard Mr. Mesic say that Croatia is now a state in which the rule of law prevails. How do you explain the fact that people are afraid to say that they were in camps, people who live there? Is that to say that they are not sure of their safety even nowadays if they're afraid to speak about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were in camps are afraid to speak about this because they are afraid that those who kept them in these camps could harm them until the present day. There is still fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say something about what you learned concerning the treatment, the treatment of people in these camps, how they were treated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they were tortured, that they were beaten with electric wires, that electric current went through them, that they made each other cut their ears off and that the other person was supposed to eat the other person's ear, that there were beatings, that there were killings. That's what happened in Pakrac Ka Poljana. And in Pakrac, they were beaten, they were tied up to radiators, they were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them survived and how many were killed in these camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for figures, I really cannot speak about that, because the exact number of persons killed is not known. These numbers are still being dealt with. The number of missing persons is going up day after day. As people are returning, everybody is looking for their own family members, and there are still quite a few who are missing. I don't know about the survivors either. People left and they went to different places, so it is hard now that the situation hasn't been fully stabilised yet, it's hard to tell. I don't really want to make any estimates of this kind because it concerns human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have the opportunity of talking to any one of these victims whose ears were cut off, and then they made them swallow these ears, and people who were burned by electric current and beaten up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to one person. They fired a gunshot through his stomach. He talked to me about that. And also another one who buried others, but they are still afraid to testify about that in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this other person buried those who did not survive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us with this: When was all this occurring? You're describing these incidents in prison camps. Again, what period would we be talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened sometime from August 1991 until the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what was the situation in Pakrac at the time? Because you've described various Serb takeovers and that sort of thing. What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 19th of August, in the town of Pakrac, Serbs were only on the outskirts, as for the area that they held militarily. The town itself was no man's land for a while, and afterwards it was under Croatian control all the time. So Gavrinica, that was mentioned by Mr. Milosevic, was on the side of Pakrac. The town was extensively shelled, bombed, so no one lived there except for the police station and the basement of that department store, and in the streets on the other side of the line, the area that was held by the Serbs. Life returned there only as of March 1992. It started to return, to put it that way. There were Croats there for the most part, and very, very few Serbs until 1995. And in 1995, after Operation Flash, a few Serbs returned, those who had somewhere to go back to, and they still don't live in the apartments where they lived before because they do not have the right to do that. Their apartments were taken away. Apartments were also destroyed. And then when buildings are repaired, they are being repaired and reconstructed by the European Union. And once houses are repaired, then those Serbs who applied to live in those houses can actually return there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear about this: You had direct communication. You learned about these camps for Serbs in this area of Pakrac, and torture of Serbs in 1991, while Croatia was still within the SFRY, before the international recognition, while the army was in the Croatian territory of the then Yugoslavia. They were still the one and only Yugoslav army. So all of that was taking place at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say something more specific as to who were the Serbs who were detained and tortured in camps, whose noses and ears were cut off, who were beaten up, who had gunshots fired into their stomachs? Who were these people? Were these people who had committed crimes or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were ordinary people. These were citizens from that area. Some lived in Pakrac Ka Poljana. They were taken there. And many were brought to Pakrac Ka Poljana from Zagreb and from other parts in Croatia. Also from the areas surrounding Pakrac, Daruvar, et cetera. Also from the village of Kip a group of people was brought to Pakrac Ka Poljana. They were not criminals in any way, nor were they doing anything against the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of this, one may infer that they were beaten up, massacred, killed, only because they were Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said just now that a number of people returned but that some people still do not live in their apartments even though their apartments were not destroyed. Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When war broke out, all the Serbs who had fled from their apartments and did not live there during the war lost the right to return to their own apartments. That is this so-called tenancy right that prevailed before, and this law is still in force, namely, that Serbs do not have the right to apartments. Efforts are being made to have this returned. I don't know when this will happen, but serious efforts are being made in order to have these tenancy rights restored. So they lost the right to live in the apartments where they had lived before, and this is a serious existential problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this law passed, that the Serbs did not have a right to return to their apartments, the apartments that they left because of what you just described now, the kind of things that happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether this was in 1992 or in 1995. I don't know exactly, to tell you the truth, because I was reintegrated in 1995. I don't know, but I think the law had already been passed by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in the present-day state of Croatia, where the rule of law prevails, this law is still in force and Serbs still cannot return to their apartments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they cannot. Some were bought, some were given to others and others are empty.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the question of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Refugees from Slavonia, Bosnia, when they got Croatian citizenship, they moved into these apartments because other citizens of Croatia who did not have apartments bought these apartments and now own them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter said that they couldn't hear your question before. Could you slow down, please, and put a pause between the question and answer. Mr. Witness too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Kwon. I thought that I was bearing this in mind, but I shall pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me something else now. You've just described this for me, what was going on in Pakrac. Can you tell me something else? I don't really want to read this again, and you heard this and you said it was correct. These camps in Slavonska Pozega, for Serbs, of course, I'm asking about that, those camps, do you have any knowledge about that, about the number of Serbs who were interned in these camps and how they were treated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge. I don't have any knowledge concerning the number of people who were there. What I heard was that they were also beaten and tortured. At that time, that seemed to be some kind of a rule between these two sides that were in conflict around Pakrac in Western Slavonia, that on the Serb side, the Croats were beaten up and tortured; and then on the Croatian side, that's what happened to the Serbs. I don't know what kind of contacts and relations they had, but one could come to the conclusion that this was really known about everyone who ever was detained. Well, not everyone, but almost everyone. So then this gave rise to tensions and also to a wish to revenge the situation that happened. So that's what happened in Pakrac and the surrounding area. I don't know about the numbers involved in Pozega. I just know that they were really beaten up badly. And I know that there were frequent exchanges between the Serb side and the Croat side, that the Croats exchanged Serbs and the Serbs exchanged Croats. So they each took their own prisoners out for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I read out only part of this to you, this list of prisons for the Serbs. How many Serb prisons were there for Croats, ones that you know about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I enumerated in Western Slavonia was Mijokovicevo, Bucje, Vocin, down in Okucani. These were prisons. And then -- well, I know about these prisons. And the rest were conflicts and killings, like Balinci, Cetekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you know of these four; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how many Croats were in these four prisons that were held by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that figure either. It's very hard for me to say, especially for Stara Gradiska. And up there at Bucje, I really don't like to make estimates. We're talking about human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in 1991, in October, you lived in Bucje for some 30 days or so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not only in Bucje, but at Bucje too. Not only in Bucje, but also in the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's where the prison was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you lived there for 30 days and you saw that prison. So this is a prison where Serbs held Croats. I assume, in view of the office that you held, that you had to have been informed as to what was going on in this prison, how many people there were there, who these people were, and how they were treated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you are referring to the office I held, let me inform you once again, if you do not remember. I did not have any authority up there whatsoever. There was only military authority up there, namely, the Territorial Defence. It was operating up there. And I did not have the possibility or the right, as they had put it, to meddle in things that I was not supposed to be interested in, according to them. So I don't know how many people were in this prison. I know that there were civilians, for the most part, those who had been collected near the separation line, and perhaps there were a small number of soldiers who had been taken prisoner during the war. Among these prisoners, there were Serbs as well. And I heard from them the most that they had been beaten up, and some were taken away and killed. But I could not really have insight into this because this was under the control of the Territorial Defence, which throughout the war that was taking place there, was violently opposed to me, so I did not have any right to access the area or enter it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, but it is highly unlikely that you couldn't really get any information, because among local people, one usually knows everything. You know what other people are cooking for lunch let alone how many people are in prison and what's going on in that prison. How many persons were there in that prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you a number that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you probably saw the building. Were you in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come close to the building, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you don't even know what the building looks like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the maximum number of people who could have been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps around 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were Serbs and how many were Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 10 were Serbs and the rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers, how many civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not pursue this any further. When you talk about events in Pakrac, on page 4, in the last paragraph, you explained that the municipality of Pakrac made a decision to remain in Yugoslavia if Croatia were to leave Yugoslavia. Is it the population itself that reached that decision or did you organise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the decision of the assembly of the municipality of Pakrac, not of the population, but of the delegates of the population of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody suggest that you should make this kind of decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the disassociation, when Croatia disassociated from Yugoslavia. That's when the Serbs voted that they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia. This was some kind of a political gesture, to make it known that people did want to stay in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, as far as I can understand this, this was not within the referendum that you had had before that; is that right? Was it before or after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first referendum was for cultural autonomy, in 1990. This was sometime around the 21st or 22nd of February, 1991. And the second referendum was to remain in Yugoslavia. That was on the 12th of May, 1991. So that was between the two referendums.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me: What was the substance of this referendum for cultural autonomy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be aware of the details now. It was a long time ago. But it was cultural and political autonomy of the Serbs in Croatia that was referred to. This was supposed to protect Serb identity in Croatia. I don't really know about the details of this referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did this mean education in the Serb language, the use of the Cyrillic alphabet, the functioning of the Serb Cultural Society of Prosvjeta? So equal treatment, actually, in terms of the protection of national identity of the Serbs, in terms of their cultural needs, then also in the fields of education, culture, et cetera. Is that what it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is the right way to put it, to protect Serb cultural identity, not to mention all these things that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that after that there was great pressure exerted? What do you know, for example, about the dismissal of Serbs from the police force, from all public services, from the media, from the health service, and so on, in Croatia in the course of 1990, when there were still no conflicts or clashes? Can you tell me something about that? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the time that the dismissal started, especially from the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. I apologise. Mr. Kwon, I won't speed up. But let me just add something. When you say "at the beginning there were dismissals from the police force," what do you mean "beginning"? When was this beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you an exact date, but I think it was the end of 1990. That's when dismissals from the police force started and from state public services, when Serbs were let go. Because it was considered there were more than was necessary by virtue of the ethnic representation, especially in the police and public services, and especially in municipalities where the HDZ won the majority in the elections. Later on, in 1991, this took hold and there were more and more dismissals from work after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have an idea as to how many people at the beginning and before the conflict broke out, how many Serbs were dismissed from the police force, from public services, from the media, and from the other jobs that they held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a figure, and I don't have an estimate either, because when all this was going on, it created great tension. And I can't make assessments of that kind. I can't hazard a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but do you have any knowledge about other areas except for the police force, health service, public services? Were Serbs dismissed from companies and enterprises, from commercial organisations, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That came later. I heard about that in the course of 1991, especially in Zagreb and in the larger towns, where there were many large enterprises. I heard that they had been dismissed just for being Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just for being Serbs, no other reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I heard from the people who were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was the people who were fired who told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that for the most part all the directors, the company managers or people who had positions of leadership in the economy, who were Serbs, ethnic Serbs, that they were dismissed straight away, or rather, replaced straight away? Some of them might have carried on doing some work in the companies, but they were replaced in their post of director or manager. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear of things like that happening too, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was going on in all these areas; police, public services, the media, the health service, and so on and so forth? Did this take on the form of a general all-out discrimination of Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did take on those proportions. It did become an all-out general discrimination, and the Serbs were afraid that they would lose their jobs. That happened principally in areas where Serbs were the minority, that is to say, in Zagreb, Sisak, Pozega, and those towns towards Bjelovar and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that happened where Serbs were really in the minority. That is where the discriminatory measures were greatest, most widespread; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's right. Where the HDZ had won the majority vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that means where the HDZ won, the programme was to dismiss the Serbs and expel them; is that so or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that was their programme, but I do know that that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you heard for the first time of instances and cases where people were taken away, where there were illegal and unlawful arrests, that all trace was lost of people, that they were being killed, from Zagreb to Vukovar, in the different places in that area, when did you first hear of that happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first heard that in mid-1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quoted something this morning, a report, and Mesic confirmed that he found it when he assumed his post of president. It dates back to 1991. It was Herzog, Tudjman's advisor, who talks about unlawful arrests of Serbs, unlawful detention of Serbs, he means arrest of Serbs - I don't have to translate from the Croatian into the Serbian language for you - and that all traces are lost of them, that it is not known whether they are alive or dead. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was -- did that report -- was that report made public after the arrival of the new authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know anything about it. Now, let's try and move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, please: After the famous barricades were set up, is it true that you established that the government in Serbia, the government in Belgrade, had nothing to do with or knowledge of that before this appeared in the public information media, and this kind of resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you when you said whether we had established this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the government in Belgrade had nothing to do or any knowledge about this? And I'm thinking of your own statement. But answer the question. You know what you said; I don't have to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was done by the local population, at their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Pakrac police set up barricades during the night but the JNA demanded that they be removed. Members of the MUP of Croatia took advantage of this and on the 2nd of March, 1991, they entered the town, exchanged gunfire with the Pakrac policemen, which means that they shot at each other, they disarmed a few of them, and in the meantime, the JNA arrived and negotiations started between the JNA and the MUP of Croatia. Two days later, the disarmament process started of the rest of the members of the Pakrac police force and the weapons were returned back to the police. Then you go on to say four assistants of Petar Gracanin, the federal Minister for Internal Affairs, arrived in Pakrac. I remember that one of them said that the -- that Croatia was a legal state and that the Pakrac policemen had to return the weapons, otherwise they would be arrested by the federal police force and that they would be turned over to the MUP of Croatia. The Serbs in Pakrac were -- saw that everything had calmed down and were disillusioned. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, how did the barricades come to be set up in the first place? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said that in private session, that I explained that in private session, so can I repeat it in a private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought we had returned to open session a long time ago. I thought we were already in open session, Mr. May, quite some time ago, because the witness only had several facts to give us in private session. I cannot waste time and go back to the questions I've already asked, that we've already covered, but I do like to know -- and I do think that too much insistence is made on these closed sessions, private sessions, because it is not the witness C-037 that is endangered by the publication of what we're talking about because everybody knows who he is anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this red/white, and white/red chequerboard was found on the death camps of Jasenovac, likes of Jasenovac, for example? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you then consider that it was only the elderly people, as you say, the older generations, who were troubled and upset by that? Do you think they had reason, good reason to be upset and troubled, and was there good reason for them to be anxious and even afraid of what was in store for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what we were saying a moment ago, discussing a moment ago, about the camps, the dismissals, the beatings up and killings and so on and so forth, was that confirmation that their fears were justified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes, because those were the first steps taken to instil fear in the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the region of Western Slavonia had deep scars, was deeply scarred by the mass crimes committed during World War II and that the people there had to be sensitive, quite justifiably so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a Serb family, a single Serb family in that part of the world which did not have casualties of some kind in World War II, during World War II? Let me stop there and then I'll continue and I'll go on to ask another question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- I don't know. Likely -- not likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia, with the exception of those who had fled before the clashes started, was there a family that did not lose somebody in these attacks launched by the Croatian police and army on Serb settlements and Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you repeat that question? I didn't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that part of the world, that is to say, in Western Slavonia, in that region, is there any family which has not lost any -- which did not lose anybody in the attacks 1991, up to 1995, in Western Slavonia, except for those who had fled before 1991 and gone to Serbia or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of the Serb families fought in the Croatian army and were there together, so such families do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but are there many such families?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this event, as far as I was able to follow and gather - and this is on page 5, paragraph 5 of your statement - you say that in the information media --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I note you are quoting the witness's written statement several times, a number of times, so it seems that your intention -- it is your intention to continuously quote his statement. Do you like us to have one? We don't have them right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is his statement, the one that I was given by you. I assume that it was included in the materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You refer to "you." Remember that we're the Judges. The Prosecution sent you that document. We had nothing to do with that, and we don't have them. Now, you were asked by the Judge: Do you want us to have the copies or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do, but as far as I recall, so far you always had copies of statements, looked at them, looked for sentences and were able to find them. So I would ask myself now why, and is this a logical mistake, that you don't have them now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have the statements. We've told you this before: We don't have the statements of the witnesses unless they're disclosed under the Rule, which, as you know, allows for the admissibility of written statements. We have those, but the other statements we don't have. Let us have a copy of these ones and we'll give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I should like to have this introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I gather there are six statements. Which is the one that you've been relying on, Mr. Milosevic? We've got it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour, I can be of assistance. Maybe Mr. Milosevic refers to the proofing summary. That is something you have in front of you, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the proofing summary, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the witness's statement of the 19th of March. No. I apologise. Of 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of May, 1990 -- no, sorry, 2002. That's the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a summary. Yes, we've got that. Thank you. Yes, we've got this one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. May I proceed, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. C-037, you say that in the media, the events that we have just described, partly in private and partly in open session, were represented as dramatic events, and this is your opinion. Don't you think that this kind of event in Pakrac is dramatic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but what was said in the media was that people had been killed, and even their names were mentioned, and this did not happen. That's why I said that these events were misrepresented.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever manage to find out who produced this report? Was it given by someone from Pakrac or did somebody in the media make it up? I mean the report about the people who were killed and that this was not true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, a journalist arrived and wrote the article from Pakrac, the report, from Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was somebody who came to Pakrac, observed the sporadic shooting and the conflict, and wrote an article about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you say there was no reason for the Serbs to flee because there was no threat to them from the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you. You say, in fact, there was no reason to leave because there was no military threat from the Croatian side in November/December 1991. So this is late 1991. And then ... Yes. You say there was no reason for the Serbs to leave because there was no military threat from the Croatian side. And then you mention the amendments. This is on page 18, the second paragraph from the bottom of your statement. You said: I was able to see that people were being manipulated in Western Slavonia, for example, in the SDS. And that's your party, is it not? Wanted to study the amendments to the Croatian constitution. People didn't want to listen but demanded weapons because they had heard rumours that the Croats had armed. So they had heard rumours that the Croats had armed. Were these rumours true? Were the Croats armed or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your first and second comments, you mixed up two events. First you spoke of late 1991 and then you spoke of early 1991. These two events were nine months apart. To respond to your first comment, in late 1991, when people were withdrawing from Grubisno Polje, Daruvar and other municipalities, there was not a strong concentration of the Croatian army, so the pressure was not so great. They were not withdrawing because of the military strength of the other side. In Daruvar, they entered Serbian villages only some five or six days later, and then destroyed and burnt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did this happen precisely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Daruvar retreated around the 15th of November, and they entered it some five days later, five or six. So it may have been the 15th, the 20th. I don't know the exact day. But there was no fighting in those villages. People withdrew from the villages, out of fear, because there were rumours of heavy concentrations of Croatian forces. And people did not have enough self-confidence, enough self-reliance. There was no JNA there. They were expecting help from the JNA. And as they were there on their own for days and days, they retreated. After that, the Croatian forces entered. Whether these were the home guard or the Croatian army or what they were called, I don't know, but they entered all the villages in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These villages then were looted for days. They were torched for days. The better houses that could not be torched were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the better houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would not burn, so they were blown up with explosives, and that's what happened to all the villages that had been controlled by the Serbs during the war. As for the second part of your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's stay with the first part for a while. That's why I'm asking you this, because it seems illogical when you say that they had no reason to be anxious and to flee, when you yourself say that once they had fled from the Croatian forces, these villages were first looted and then burnt or blown up. Does that not contradict what you said, namely, that they had nothing to fear, nothing to flee from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces that entered these villages were not strong enough to take these villages from the local Serbs. A single man can torch a house or a village. I don't know how many of them came in later, but had they had strong forces, they would have entered the villages on the same day that the Serbs left them. But the villages were not looted and burnt in a single day. This went on for days and days. So there was time for more people to arrive. Maybe some civilians took part in this. That's why I'm saying there was no reason to abandon the area. People could have held it and gone on living there. But I think the local commanders were not up to the task; they panicked and they manipulated the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they manipulated people into fleeing instead of fighting; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they should have stayed there and preserved their village rather than leaving it. That's my opinion, still. As for the other question you put to me, when the videotape of Spegelj was published, was broadcast, it terrified people because they concluded that the Croats were arming, and felt unsafe. When the amendments to the constitution were discussed in Okucani, when Mr. Kosutic came there to help us, you couldn't even talk to people about the constitutional amendments. They were not interested in that. All they wanted was weapons. They said: If I have a gun, I feel safe. And this was a widespread phenomenon. The fear was such that they demanded weapons, and there was pressure on all the political leaders to do this. Those who refused were considered to be traitors. It was thought that they were not looking after the people properly. Later on, in June 1991, when the event at Borovo Selo took place, I think it was - yes - in May, on my way back, passing through the Croatian villages from Osijek to Slavonska Pozega, I saw people going out at night carrying rifles, so I saw that the Croats were also armed. I don't know who of the Croats was armed, on what basis, how, whether it was just members of the HDZ or whether it was also other people, but I did see them carrying weapons. And then at the same time the Serbs armed themselves as well. Some people bought weapons initially. I don't know who supplied them, but a lot of weapons were bought, and many people armed themselves. This was a widespread phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the point in time when the National Guard Corps, as it was called, was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in the summer of 1991, but I don't have the exact information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were members of this National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was volunteers or policemen. I'm not sure exactly. I know it was established and that its name was the National Guard Corps, but I don't know who the recruits were. I don't know from where these people were recruited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have described camps where people were tortured, people fleeing and torching of houses and villages. Now I have a general question for you. After the first day of your testimony, a newspaper said that Witness C-037 accused Milosevic of planning the Karlovac-Karlobag-Virovitica boundary. Since I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that doesn't sound like a very correct question. What you can do is ask the witness about his evidence, not about the way in which some newspaper has reported it. Now, what is the correct question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm asking the witness whether he accused me in his testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. It doesn't matter. What he said is what he said. It's not for the witness to comment on it. You can do so in due course and we can make a finding about it. It's not for him to comment now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, don't argue. Just move on to the next point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him some question which is relevant to the evidence, but asking him about the newspaper report is not either -- or asking him to comment on his own evidence, which is what you appear to be doing. Now, that is simply not permissible. Now, what's the point -- what is the point you want to make? If you tell us the point, maybe we can formulate it into a question which is permissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you, Mr. May, if you will allow me. I assume I have the right to put questions in connection with exhibits shown to the witness who was asked to comment on them. If an exhibit was shown to a witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Of course you're entitled to do that. Put the -- let's go to the exhibit. Put the exhibit -- the right way to do it is put the exhibit to him and then you can ask your question. Now, which is the exhibit you want to ask him about? If you don't know which one it is, we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a map of Croatia on which there were two straight lines, or rather, one broken straight line, marking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's identify the exhibit. We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to be tab 3 of Exhibit 326. Is this the one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes. This map was shown. Please put it on the projector. I can see it even from here. I'm sure the witness can see it, if it's only 50 centimetres away. So put it on the projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There, you see this map, Mr. C-037?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This map was shown to you here. What connection does it have with any standpoint of Belgrade? If you know, tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with Seselj's slogan, Karlobag, Karlovac, Virovitica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Leave Seselj's slogan alone. Various politicians say various things at different points in time. Did you ever hear a single representative of the government -- as you know, Seselj was in the opposition. Did you ever hear a single representative of the government, starting with me in Serbia, or the Prime Minister or a minister, or someone from Yugoslavia, a general, for example, talking about a plan, an alleged plan, such as the one shown to you on this map? Did anyone ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. It's an important point. There's no point if you go on; he can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear it from any officials of the government of Serbia or the government of Yugoslavia. I said what this line, this boundary, was connected with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So can we take it, Witness 37, that you never heard anybody in the government talking about this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But as I recollect it, you said that you saw somebody - I may be wrong about this -- remind us, if you would, what your evidence was that you say connects this line with the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps with the sentence that all the Serbs would live in a single state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but how is that connected with this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I linked this sentence with Mr. Milosevic, that all the Serbs would live in one state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me finish. It doesn't explain quite why you come to this particular -- why this particular line on the map. What's the significance of it? Would you explain to us. I know you say it's connected with Greater Serbia, but can you help us as to this or not? It may be you can't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This here is the Krajina. This is Western Slavonia. Seselj came to visit Krajina and Western Slavonia and he spoke about this border, about this line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's what Seselj says. I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seselj said that in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did he have some kind of a political party then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he perhaps in parliament?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I am. The radical party --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he in opposition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whose opposition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how can you say, then, even if he had spoken about this - I don't even know that he had - how can you link this up with some position of the government of Serbia or any position of mine? Because somebody, according to you, said something at some point, some person from the opposition.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I am linking that to his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right. I don't know if he said that, but over here, during your testimony, this was linked up to me. It's being held against me. So as you can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... trouble what anybody is putting in the papers. It's what the evidence is here of which we shall be the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that sentence that many are abusing here, "All Serbs in a single state," does not say "will" but was linked to the following explanation: That Yugoslavia was in the interests of all Yugoslav peoples and that Serbs had a particular interest in the preservation of Yugoslavia because only with the existence of Yugoslavia can the Serbs live in one state, although they are in different republics? Do you know that? Do you know how come this quotation was distorted, that it pertains to that one and only state, Yugoslavia, the then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not correct the quotation or distort it, believe me. I am telling you, I just know that the Serbs wanted to remain in Yugoslavia, to live in that state. As for this line, I linked it up to the statement of that man, not to go into all of that again. And I don't know about these changes and these inversions, what you said, I mean "will" or "do" or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you are interpreting it that way. The Serbs did live in one state while Yugoslavia was still in existence, but also all Croats lived in one state. Because they even have problems now, Croats in Bosnia, greater problems than they ever thought they would have, because slowly, under pressure, they are not sending children to Sarajevo to go to school. They're sending them to Split or to Zagreb. All the Croats lived in one state too, and the Muslims lived in one state too. That's why I said that for all Yugoslav peoples, Yugoslavia is the solution, because they all live in one state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've been asked: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You uttered that sentence, which is very correct and very humane and very reasonable, but you linked that up with some speech. You even said that this was in Kosovo Polje, this speech. This speech in Kosovo Polje is a remarkable speech, and it is quite contrary to what is being asserted here, and everybody had the right to read it. So who put this into your head, that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, you can't go on making these speeches. Now, you can give evidence in due course and you can tell us about it then. Now, have you got any other questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, of course. Well, I have three hours left for tomorrow, Mr. May. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get on with it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I am going on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So regardless of the fact that there was no military danger involved as far as the Serbs from Croatia were concerned, in your opinion, and it was obvious that they were endangered indeed, that all their villages were torched, et cetera, and they all had to flee, and you seem to be saying that they should have stayed there and fought because then they would have kept their houses, then probably somebody would have accused them too of carrying out an aggression against their own houses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You're supposed to be giving evidence, although it may not appear like that. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, I still think that there was no reason for them to leave. I believe that. Because there are reasons why I'm saying this. Where the Serbs were in Croatia, in their own villages, and where there were no conflicts, the villages remained intact. Had Serbs not left then, as they stayed behind from Pakrac further down, these villages remained. I am not justifying this. This was a retaliation. This was a crime committed against these people. But I repeat: There was no concentration of forces. There was not that kind of threat that was supposed to make them leave. And I know, on the other hand, that there was no goodwill for the Serbs to remain. But one cannot live on the goodwill of others only. One has to live on the basis of one's own free will and to stay where they are and fight. I did not mean that they should fight in the sense of committing crimes or something like that, but defending themselves. I think that then Croatia would not have entered Western Slavonia. What was done against it afterwards is a different story altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is your explanation. In Croatia, did the Serbs do anything else but defend themselves in the territory where they had lived for several centuries? Did they go to conquer Croat territories, or were they defending the territories where they lived, territories that were theirs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, down there, around Drnis, there were conquests of Croatian villages that did not belong to the Serbs, that did not belong to the Serbs. Also there were some in Kordun or in Banija. I can't recall exactly now. The problem is that in those areas where the Serbs did exercise their own control, they should not have torched Croat villages. And they should not have expelled or killed Croat civilians who were there, because that happened too. I'm not trying to say that there was not ethnic distrust among them, but that's not right. Like Donji Caglic near Pakrac, when the army came, there were one or ten, I don't know how many extremists, but others were not. They could have remained alive. Because if you are involved in a struggle of defence to live in your own home, that does not give you the right to expel others. And now everybody is trying to justify themselves that way when they say that's why I committed something bad against someone else. I think that sufficient attempts were not made to avoid this evil, and I have reason to think this way. I was born in Croatia. My parents were born in Croatia. They also lived through the Second World War. Their entire families, all their relatives, were killed. As children, they were in Ustasha camps. But it was Croats who saved them from these Ustasha camps. So in our history, we have cases when we were killing each other, but there are also cases when we were saving, rescuing each other, and I think it was more difficult to do it then than it is now. I live in the conviction that we Serbs should have done even more in order to prevent this from happening. That is my conviction. I cannot change it. I know what kind of state this is, and I know the fears involved, and I saw my own father, who was afraid, and he said, "Yes, the Ustasha killed all the members of my family, all my relatives, but it is Croats who saved me from the camp." And he was 12 years old, he was not 30 years old. He was a child, a 12-year-old child, but he was aware of that. And also in that war, they joined the Croats and they joined the Partizans. And we did not give each other a chance to resolve things and not slaughter each other. That's what I keep thinking about time and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: C-037, I think that your way of thinking is right, and I think that no one can or has the right to kill another person because he himself is exposed to danger unless he is saving his own life, unless this is self-defence. As for these excesses that you are referring to, you mentioned a village near Drnis and you mentioned something else near Benkovac, et cetera. But you did not answer my question: Is it correct, along with the exceptions that nobody can or should justify, nor would anybody accept this kind of justification. So given these exceptions, is it correct that in those years of crisis, Serbs, for the most part, that is to say as a rule, exclusively defended their own doorstep and the territories where they lived, along with these excesses that nobody is justifying. But generally speaking, isn't it correct that they were defending their own villages, their own homes, their own doorsteps where they were imperilled? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's clarify that. As for crimes, nobody is justifying that. The Croatian parliament, in 1990, adopted an amendment to this - what's it called? - 68 and abolished the Cyrillic alphabet; is that right? What was the reaction in Western Slavonia to this? Do you think that this evolution in the atmosphere of fear started escalating, I mean with these first seemingly not exactly dramatic changes but basically, and over the longer term, dramatic changes. Tell me about the atmosphere then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This did sound negative among the Serb population, because they were building Croatia together with the Croats. They were constituent people. And the alphabet had a footing -- was on a footing of equality. And they wanted their alphabet to be equal, because that is a right that had been acquired, and that is something that they had lived with for years. So this upset them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, they can't hear the question. You've got to leave a pause. And this must be the last question before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The events that followed later, after this first alarm, so to speak, did they escalate further into an atmosphere of fear and threat that you reacted to, as you had put it yourself, spontaneously and on the basis of the feelings of the citizens themselves there where they lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially when the Serbs were no longer a constituent people, when they became a minority. And when they were becoming a minority people, felt that in this way they were considered to be of minor value. And before that, it was said that they were privileged and whatever. So they took this to be an attack against them, as a rise in discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must adjourn now because the tape is about to run out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one thing. I have to apologise for my mistake that, with the assistance of Madam Registrar, I realise that it was not the proof summary that the accused is quoting, and the written statement is dated 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of May. So we had better have one, if the Prosecution -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now, 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 4th day of October 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.15 p.m.
